title: Shankara, Ramanuja, Madhva
bigQuestion: How can three careful commentators read the same sacred words and reach three different accounts of God, the self and the world?

story.title: Four Words, Three Readings
story.kicker: Three teachers, centuries apart, write three commentaries on the same short phrase.
paragraphs: Imagine a long table in a library. On it lie three old books, each a commentary in Sanskrit on the Upanishads. Each author lived in South India, but centuries apart: Shankara around the 8th century, Ramanuja around the 11th and 12th, and Madhva around the 13th. Each book stops at the same passage in the Chandogya Upanishad: sa atma tat tvam asi, "that is the self; that art thou."

Shankara reads the phrase as a plain statement of identity. The self you truly are, beneath body and mind, is not other than Brahman, the one reality. The sense of being a separate person, he argues, belongs to ignorance, and knowledge removes it the way light removes the fear of a rope mistaken for a snake.

Ramanuja reads the same words differently. "That" is Brahman, and "thou" is also Brahman, but Brahman as the inner controller of the self, the way a soul lives within a body. The self is real and distinct, yet it exists only as part of Brahman's body. Unity and difference are both true.

Madhva reads the Sanskrit sounds another way. In the joined words sa atma tat tvam asi, he and his followers also find the possible division atat tvam asi: "thou art not that." The self is always distinct from God, who is Vishnu, independent and supreme. The self depends on God entirely but is never the same as God.

All three men were brilliant, devout and careful with language. Each founded a lasting tradition that is alive today in temples, monasteries and homes. This chapter asks how the genre of commentary works, and how the same verse can open into three paths.
story.think: If three expert readers disagree about four words, what does that suggest about reading sacred texts? Is disagreement a failure, or part of the tradition?

lessons.title: What a Bhashya Does
lessons.mainIdea: A bhashya is a formal commentary that explains a root text line by line and argues for one reading against others.
reading: In Sanskrit learning, the great teachers rarely wrote brand-new books from nothing. Instead they wrote a *bhashya*, a commentary on an older text held to be authoritative. A bhashya quotes a line of the root text, explains its words and grammar, and then draws out its meaning. It often argues against rival readings by stating their case first and then answering it.

This method is called purvapaksha and siddhanta. The purvapaksha is the opponent's view, stated fairly and often strongly. The siddhanta is the author's settled conclusion. Good commentators took their opponents seriously, since a weak summary would make their own answer look weak. Students today can learn from this habit of fair statement.

Commentaries then gathered their own commentaries. A student of Shankara's school might read a sub-commentary on his commentary on the Upanishads. The result is a long *conversation* across centuries. Each school's teachers built on the founder's work, and each school's texts answered the others by name.

words.d: a formal Sanskrit commentary that explains a root text and argues for a reading
the opponent's position, stated first in a debate or commentary
the settled conclusion the commentator argues for
the older authoritative text on which a commentary is written

look.title: State It Fairly First
look.text: A commentator writes: "Some say the self is simply one with Brahman. They argue from 'That art thou.' This is their strongest point." Only then does the commentator give his own answer.
look.prompt: Why might stating the opposing view well make an argument stronger, not weaker? How could you use this method in your own essay?

choices: A formal commentary on a root text
check.why: A bhashya explains a root text and argues for one reading.

choices: The first verse of a hymn

choices: Rules required them to lose debates

check.why: A strong answer requires a fair statement of the other side.

lessons.title: The Triple Foundation
lessons.mainIdea: Vedanta teachers wrote on three root texts together: the Upanishads, the Bhagavad Gita and the Brahma Sutras.
reading: Vedanta teachers speak of the *prasthana traya*, the "triple foundation" or three starting points. They are the Upanishads, the Bhagavad Gita and the Brahma Sutras. A teacher who wished to found a school of Vedanta was expected to comment on all three, showing that his reading made sense of each one.

The Upanishads were regarded as shruti, revealed texts. The Gita, part of the Mahabharata, belongs to smriti, "what is remembered," but it was treasured as a summary of Upanishadic teaching. The *Brahma Sutras*, credited by tradition to Badarayana, are about 550 short aphorisms that organize the Upanishads' teaching into a system.

The Brahma Sutras are so brief that they cannot be understood without a commentary. Scholars date them roughly to the early centuries CE, though estimates vary widely. Because they are so compressed, each school reads them to support its own view. That is why the same three texts could found several different philosophies.

words.d: the triple foundation of Vedanta: Upanishads, Gita and Brahma Sutras
short aphorisms credited to Badarayana that organize Upanishadic teaching
"what is remembered"; authoritative texts such as the epics, held below shruti
a very short saying that packs in an idea; a sutra

check.why: These three are the triple foundation of Vedanta.

check.why: The sutras are compressed aphorisms that require explanation.

lessons.title: Not Two
lessons.mainIdea: Shankara taught Advaita, non-dualism: the self is not other than Brahman, and the sense of separateness comes from ignorance.
reading: Shankara, or Adi Shankaracharya, is dated by most scholars to about the 8th century CE. Traditional accounts say he was born in Kerala, traveled all over India, debated other schools and died young. Some lineages give earlier dates. He is the most famous teacher of *Advaita* Vedanta, the school of "non-dualism."

Advaita teaches that Brahman, pure being, awareness and bliss, is the one reality. The self, atman, is not other than Brahman. Our ordinary sense that we are separate persons in a world of many things is due to *avidya*, ignorance. Shankara compares it to seeing a rope in dim light and mistaking it for a snake. When a lamp is brought, the snake was never there.

Shankara does not say the world is nothing. At the level of everyday life it is real enough, and duties and worship matter. But from the highest standpoint, he teaches, only Brahman is ultimately real. Later Advaitins used the word *maya* for the power by which the one appears as many. Advaita followers hold that liberation, moksha, comes through knowledge that removes ignorance.

words.d: "non-dualism"; Shankara's school, teaching that self and Brahman are not two
ignorance; in Advaita, what makes the self seem separate from Brahman
in later Advaita, the power by which the one reality appears as many
liberation from the cycle of rebirth

look.title: The Rope and the Snake
look.text: In dim light, a traveler sees a snake on the path and freezes in fear. A lamp is brought. There is only a rope. The fear was real; the snake never was.
look.prompt: In Shankara's image, what is the rope, what is the snake, and what is the lamp? What does the image say about how liberation happens?

check.q: What does Advaita mean?
check.why: A-dvaita means not two.

check.q: In Shankara's image, what removes the snake?
check.why: Knowledge, like light, removes the mistaken perception.

check.q: What does Advaita say causes the sense of being separate from Brahman?
check.why: Advaita locates separateness in ignorance.

lessons.title: Shankara Reads "That Art Thou"
lessons.mainIdea: Shankara reads tat tvam asi as identity: stripped of limits, the self and Brahman are one and the same.
reading: For Shankara, tat tvam asi is a *mahavakya*, a great saying that teaches identity. "That" refers to Brahman, the cause of the universe. "Thou" refers to the individual self. On the surface they seem different: Brahman is all-knowing and infinite, the self limited and struggling.

Shankara's school explains the phrase with an example. When someone says, "This is that Devadatta I met years ago," we set aside the differences of time and place and recognize the same person. So too, set aside the limits of "that" and "thou," and what remains is one pure awareness. Shankara holds this is what the Upanishad intends.

Advaita followers see this reading as the plain sense of the Upanishads. Critics from other schools argue that it makes the personal God, worship and the world less than ultimately real. Advaitins reply that worship is valuable and prepares the mind for knowledge. The debate between these positions has continued for more than a thousand years.

words.d: a great saying of the Upanishads, such as tat tvam asi
being one and the same
upadhi: a condition, like a body, that makes the one seem limited

look.title: Shankara on the Great Saying
look.text: Shankara explains that in "That art thou," the qualities that make Brahman seem distant and the self seem small are set aside; what remains is the one self, and knowing this is liberation.
look.cite: Shankara, commentary on Chandogya Upanishad 6.8.7 and Upadeshasahasri (c. 8th c.), paraphrased
look.prompt: Which words in the phrase does Shankara say must be "set aside"? Why is that step needed for his reading to work?

check.q: How does Shankara read tat tvam asi?
choices: As the self being a part of Brahman's body
As identity of self and Brahman
check.why: Shankara reads identity; Ramanuja relation; Madhva difference.

check.q: What is the Devadatta example meant to show?
choices: Setting aside differences of time and place to recognize the same thing
check.why: The example shows identity recognized beneath different conditions.

check.q: What do critics from other schools say about Advaita?
choices: It makes the personal God and world less than ultimately real
check.why: Other schools object that Advaita diminishes God's personal reality.

lessons.title: Shankara's Legacy
lessons.mainIdea: Tradition credits Shankara with founding monasteries across India, and his teaching shaped modern Hinduism deeply.
reading: Tradition says Shankara founded four *mathas*, or monastic centers, at the four corners of India: Sringeri in the south, Dwaraka in the west, Puri in the east and Jyotirmath in the north. Scholars debate how many of these he founded himself. The heads of these mathas carry the title Shankaracharya today.

Shankara is also credited with many hymns, including devotional poems to Shiva, Vishnu and the Goddess. Scholars debate which of these he actually wrote. The tradition's picture of Shankara joins a stern philosopher of knowledge with a devout poet, and many Smarta Hindus honor him as a great teacher.

In the modern period, Advaita became very influential outside India. Swami Vivekananda presented a form of it at the World's Parliament of Religions in Chicago in 1893. Many Western readers came to think of Advaita as "the" Hindu view. Scholars caution that this is misleading, since other Vedanta schools have far larger followings among devout Hindus.

words.d: a monastic center; tradition credits Shankara with founding four
the title of the heads of the mathas in Shankara's tradition
a Hindu tradition honoring several deities, closely linked with Shankara

look.title: The Four Traditional Mathas
look.cite: Traditional account of the Shankara mathas; see scholarly discussion in standard histories of Advaita
look.prompt: Why might a tradition place its centers at four corners of a land? What does the map suggest about Shankara's aims?

check.q: What is a matha?
check.why: Tradition credits Shankara with four mathas.

check.q: Which matha is traditionally in the south?
check.why: Sringeri is in Karnataka, in the south.

check.q: Why do scholars say it is misleading to call Advaita "the" Hindu view?
choices: Advaita was never taught in India

check.why: Hinduism holds many schools; Advaita is one of them.

lessons.title: The Self as God's Body
lessons.mainIdea: Ramanuja taught Vishishtadvaita: Brahman, who is Vishnu, is one, and souls and the world are real as his body.
reading: Ramanuja is traditionally dated 1017 to 1137, though many scholars give a shorter life in the 11th and 12th centuries. He lived in Tamil Nadu and led the Sri Vaishnava community at the great temple of Srirangam. He wrote the Sri Bhashya on the Brahma Sutras and a commentary on the Gita.

His school is called *Vishishtadvaita*, "qualified non-dualism" or "non-dualism of the qualified." Brahman is one, but Brahman is qualified by, or includes, real souls and a real world. Ramanuja's key image is soul and body. As a soul lives in and controls a body, God lives in and controls all souls and the world, which make up his body.

For Ramanuja, Brahman is not an impersonal reality but a personal God, Narayana or Vishnu, full of good qualities: knowledge, power, beauty and compassion. The world is not an illusion. Souls are real, eternal and distinct, yet they cannot exist apart from God. This allowed Ramanuja to join Upanishadic philosophy with the *bhakti* of the Tamil poet-saints.

words.d: "qualified non-dualism"; Ramanuja's school
Ramanuja's commentary on the Brahma Sutras
the tradition of Vishnu devotion led by Ramanuja, centered in South India
loving devotion to God

look.title: Soul and Body
look.text: Ramanuja's analogy: your body is real and truly yours, but it lives only because you live in it and move it. So the world and all souls are real, and they are God's body, living by his presence within them.
look.prompt: How does this analogy keep both unity and difference? Which Advaita claim does it reject?

check.q: What does Vishishtadvaita mean?
check.why: Ramanuja's school is qualified non-dualism.

check.q: What is Ramanuja's key image for God and the world?
check.why: The soul-body relation is central to Ramanuja.

check.q: Which temple is associated with Ramanuja?
check.why: Ramanuja led the Sri Vaishnava community at Srirangam.

lessons.title: Ramanuja Reads the Same Words
lessons.mainIdea: Ramanuja reads tat tvam asi as God dwelling in the self, and Gita 18.66 as a call to surrender.
reading: For Ramanuja, both "that" and "thou" in tat tvam asi refer to Brahman. "That" is Brahman as cause of the world. "Thou" is Brahman as the inner controller dwelling in Shvetaketu's self. Words that name a body can also name the soul within it, and words that name a soul can name God within it. So the phrase teaches that God lives in the self, not that the self simply is God.

Ramanuja reads the Gita as a book of devotion. He takes bhakti to be a loving, constant remembrance of God that grows from knowledge and action. On Gita 18.66, "giving up all dharmas, come to me alone for refuge," his tradition sees a call to *prapatti*, complete surrender. Later Sri Vaishnava teachers called 18.66 the charama shloka, the final verse.

Ramanuja's followers see his reading as faithful to both the Upanishads and the devotional heart of the Gita. Advaitins answer that his reading adds distinctions the texts do not need. Both sides cite the same verses and argue from grammar, context and the whole sweep of scripture. That is how Vedanta debate works.

words.d: antaryamin; God as dwelling within and guiding every self
complete surrender to God, stressed in the Sri Vaishnava tradition
"the final verse"; the Sri Vaishnava name for Gita 18.66

look.title: Ramanuja on "That Art Thou"
look.text: Ramanuja explains that "thou" names the self together with the Lord who dwells within it as its inner controller; so the saying teaches that the Supreme lives in the self, not that the two are simply the same.
look.cite: Ramanuja, Sri Bhashya 1.1.1 and Vedarthasangraha (c. 12th c.), paraphrased
look.prompt: Compare this to Shankara's reading. Which word does each thinker treat differently?

check.q: For Ramanuja, what does "thou" in tat tvam asi ultimately name?
choices: Brahman dwelling in the self as inner controller
check.why: Ramanuja reads "thou" as naming God within the self.

check.q: How does Ramanuja's tradition read Gita 18.66?
choices: As a call to leave all devotion
As a rule for warriors only
As a call to prapatti, complete surrender
check.why: Sri Vaishnavas see 18.66 as teaching surrender.

check.q: What do Advaitins object to in Ramanuja's reading?
choices: It adds distinctions the texts do not need
check.why: Advaitins argue for identity without such distinctions.

lessons.title: Five Differences
lessons.mainIdea: Madhva taught Dvaita, dualism: God, souls and matter are eternally distinct, and Vishnu alone is independent.
reading: Madhva, also called Madhvacharya or Anandatirtha, lived in the 13th century; scholars often give 1238 to 1317, while his tradition gives earlier dates. He was born near Udupi in present-day Karnataka, where he established the worship of Krishna in a temple still famous today. He wrote commentaries on the Brahma Sutras, the Gita and the Upanishads.

His school is called *Dvaita*, dualism. Madhva taught five eternal differences, the pancha-bheda: between God and souls, God and matter, souls and souls, souls and matter, and matter and matter. God, Vishnu, is fully independent. Everything else is dependent on him. The world is real, and the differences in it are real.

Madhva also taught that souls differ in nature, and his tradition holds that God's grace, won through devotion, is necessary for liberation. In moksha the soul does not merge with God; it lives in joyful service and nearness to him. Madhva's followers today, including many in Karnataka and among Kannada-speaking families abroad, honor him as a great teacher of devotion.

words.d: "dualism"; Madhva's school, teaching eternal difference between God and souls
the five eternal differences taught by Madhva
town in Karnataka where Madhva established a famous Krishna temple
God's freely given help, which Madhva's tradition holds is needed for liberation

look.prompt: Which of these differences would Shankara deny at the highest level? Which would Ramanuja accept?

lessons.title: "Thou Art Not That"
lessons.mainIdea: Madhva's tradition reads the Chandogya phrase so it teaches difference, and reads the whole Upanishad through that lens.
reading: Sanskrit words often join together in writing, which can hide where one word ends and the next begins. In the Chandogya phrase sa atma tat tvam asi, Madhva's tradition finds a possible division: sa atma atat tvam asi, "that self, thou art not that." On this reading, the Upanishad teaches the self's difference from God.

Madhva also offers a second line of argument that does not rely on the split. Even if the words are read "that art thou," he argues, the phrase can mean "you are like that" or "you belong to that," in the way one might say a devoted servant is "one" with his master's purpose. He points to the Upanishad's many images that show difference, such as the bird and the tree.

Advaitins reject the split reading as forced. Madhva's followers answer that his reading fits the grammar and the whole of scripture better, and that the Upanishads' own images keep God and soul apart. As with the other schools, the argument rests on careful claims about language, context and the rest of scripture.

words.d: the joining of Sanskrit words in sound and writing, which can hide word breaks
"thou art not that"; the division of the phrase found in Madhva's tradition
careful explanation of a text, especially a sacred one

look.title: Where Does the Word Break?
look.text: Written together: saatmaatattvamasi. Divided one way: sa atma tat tvam asi, "that is the self; that art thou." Divided another way: sa atma atat tvam asi, "that self, thou art not that."
look.prompt: How can the same sounds support two readings? What else besides grammar would a commentator use to decide?

check.q: What is sandhi?
choices: The joining of Sanskrit words in sound and writing
check.why: Sandhi joins words and can hide word breaks.

check.q: How does Madhva's tradition divide the Chandogya phrase?
choices: As tat tvam asi, that art thou, meaning identity
As atat tvam asi, thou art not that
check.why: Madhva's tradition finds atat, not that.

check.q: What do Advaitins say about the split reading?
choices: It is the only correct reading

check.why: Advaitins reject the division as forced; Madhvas defend it.

lessons.title: Three Schools Side by Side
lessons.mainIdea: Laid side by side, the three schools differ on the self, the world, God and liberation, and each remains a living tradition.
reading: Setting the schools side by side helps. On the self: Shankara says it is not other than Brahman; Ramanuja says it is real and distinct but part of God's body; Madhva says it is eternally different from God. On the world: for Shankara it is real at the everyday level but not ultimately; for Ramanuja and Madhva it is fully real.

On God: for Shankara, the highest Brahman is beyond all qualities, though worship of a personal God is valuable. For Ramanuja and Madhva, the highest is the personal God Vishnu, full of good qualities. On liberation: for Shankara, knowledge removes ignorance; for Ramanuja, devotion and surrender bring God's grace; for Madhva, devotion and God's grace bring the soul near to him.

None of these schools is a relic. Each has monasteries, temples, teachers and families who follow it today, in India and in the United States. When studying them, the goal is not to pick a winner. It is to understand each teacher's reasoning well enough to explain it in terms its followers would recognize.

words.d: a tradition of interpreting the Upanishads, Gita and Brahma Sutras
God understood as having qualities, will and relationship with beings
setting positions side by side to see how they are alike and different
